paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35), or TYK2 deficiency, is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency. The first reported patient had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome and showed susceptibility to viral, fungal, and mycobacterial infections together with atopic dermatitis and elevated serum IgE (Minegishi et al., 2006). Patients reported later did not have the features of hyper-IgE syndrome, and Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infections.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, born in 1992, who was the third child of healthy first-cousin parents. He was vaccinated with BCG at 2 months of age, and at 8 months left axillary lymphadenopathy was found. He developed disseminated BCG infection with generalized fistulous lymphadenopathy and fever. He also had neurobrucellosis with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, severe sensorineural hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, and lacunar infarcts on MRI. He had pneumonia and herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve. Serum IgE measured at 2, 11, 16, and 18 years of age was normal or slightly high (80, 115, 218, and 155 IU/ml, respectively), and serum IgG, IgM, and IgA were normal. His PPD skin test was negative, and his antibody response to tetanus toxoid was low. He had no atopy or eczema, staphylococcal skin infections, skeletal or dental abnormalities, or candidiasis. Kilic et al. (2012) noted that, unlike the first Japanese TYK2-deficient patient, their patient had none of the cardinal features of hyper-IgE syndrome. They suggested that TYK2 deficiency be considered in patients with BCG disease, particularly when severe herpesvirus infections are also present, even without features of hyper-IgE syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) restudied the Japanese patient (P1) reported by Minegishi et al. (2006), a man born to consanguineous parents. He had had atopic dermatitis since 1 month of age and recurrent bacterial and viral infections since 1 year of age. These included recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, BCGitis, nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis with sepsis, parainfluenza virus 3 pneumonia, recurrent oral HSV infections, molluscum contagiosum, mild oral candidiasis, pneumonia without pneumatocele, otitis, and sinusitis. He also had ocular sarcoidosis. Repeated studies showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and high serum IgE (1,430-2,100 IU/ml).

paragraphs.text: In kindred C, a Moroccan family with consanguineous parents, P3 was a girl who was hospitalized at 13 years of age with suspected abdominal tuberculosis (Kreins et al., 2015). Her abdominal complaints persisted despite antimycobacterial treatment, and a few months later she developed ascites and a psoas abscess. Treatment was restarted, but she was readmitted with bacterial meningitis and died 15 months after symptom onset. Her younger brother (P4) was hospitalized at 8 months of age for meningitis of unknown etiology. He had recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels, but no high serum IgE. He was 15 years old, without treatment, at the time of the report.

paragraphs.text: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy, aged 1 year and 11 months, who was the second child of young nonconsanguineous parents. He was born in 2016 and vaccinated with BCG on the third day of life. He developed an abscess and ulceration at the BCG vaccination site and BCG-associated tuberculosis of the axillary lymph nodes. He had no high serum IgE, atopy, staphylococcal illness, or lymphopenia. The percentage of B cells was increased and that of NK cells was decreased. His motor development was normal, but he did not say simple words until 3 years and 4 months of age, and he had a small head circumference. Wu et al. (2020) also reviewed 12 patients with TYK2 deficiency. Of these, 58% had intracellular bacterial infections, 58% had recurrent viral infections, and 25% had markedly increased serum IgE. paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2022) studied an international cohort of 112 children hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia. Three of them were unrelated Turkish children with TYK2 deficiency, each born to a different set of consanguineous parents. P2, a 2-year-old girl, was hospitalized for moderate COVID-19 pneumonia but did not need oxygen therapy. Her earlier history included hospitalization for sepsis as a neonate, 2 ICU admissions for fever and dyspnea before 5 months of age, a diagnosis of Kawasaki disease at 11 months, and hospitalization for infection with the VZV vaccine at 2 years. P3, a 4-year-old boy, and P4, a 9-year-old boy, were both admitted to the ICU for critical COVID-19 pneumonia and needed high-flow oxygen therapy. P3 had been hospitalized for neonatal sepsis and admitted to the ICU for influenza pneumonia at 3 years. P4 had recurrent bronchitis requiring hospital admission and inhaler therapy. Neither boy had an adverse reaction to MMR vaccination. All 3 survived. P3's 3-year-old younger sister, who carried the same genotype, had a history of critical influenza pneumonia requiring intubation and ventilation and of disseminated varicella. She had not been infected with SARS-CoV-2 and remained seronegative. Zhang et al. (2022) found critical COVID-19 pneumonia in these unrelated patients surprising, because TYK2 deficiency impairs but does not abolish cellular responses to type I IFNs. They noted that more infected TYK2-deficient patients would be needed to estimate penetrance, which may be incomplete.

paragraphs.text: In a Chinese boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents, who had BCG disease, recurrent respiratory infections, Salmonella infection, and influenza virus infection without elevated IgE, Wu et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.2395G-A transition in exon 17 of the TYK2 gene, resulting in a gly799-to-arg (G799R) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. TYK2 mRNA expression was decreased in the patient's cells, and no TYK2 protein was detected. In transfected HEK293T cells, the mutation also decreased mRNA and protein expression of tagged TYK2. The variant was present in the gnomAD database.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated Turkish children born to consanguineous parents (P2, P3, and P4), Zhang et al. (2022) identified a homozygous frameshift variant in the TYK2 gene (P216Rfs*14). P2 had moderate COVID-19 pneumonia, and P3 and P4 had critical COVID-19 pneumonia. P3's younger sister, who had critical influenza pneumonia and disseminated varicella, carried the same homozygous genotype. Autosomal recessive inheritance was confirmed by family segregation analysis. The variant had previously been shown to cause loss of expression, and the authors confirmed that it was loss of function. Patient fibroblasts transduced with ACE2 did not control SARS-CoV-2 replication normally and failed to induce ISGs in response to IFN-alpha-2b.
